title: Number Patterns Grade 4: Finding the Rule (+ Free Quiz)
meta_title: Number Patterns Grade 4: Find the Rule + Quiz
meta_desc: Teach number patterns grade 4 the smart way: find the rule, use input-output tables and two-step rules, with a free 8-question quiz and printable practice.
excerpt: A pattern is not a list of numbers to memorise — it is a rule wearing a disguise. Here is how I teach Grade 4 to hunt down the rule of any sequence, read an input-output table, and handle two-step rules like ‘times 3, then add 1’, plus a quick quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Put 3, 7, 11, 15 on the board and ask a Grade 4 class what comes next. Most will get 19 — but ask them why and you learn who is really thinking. The child who says ‘it goes up by 4 each time’ has found the rule. The child who shrugs has memorised four numbers and nothing more. That gap is the whole point of number patterns grade 4: by this stage the goal is no longer to continue a sequence by feel, but to name the rule in words and then use it. A pattern, I keep telling my students, is just a rule wearing a disguise.

Grade 3 was about spotting simple growing patterns and shape patterns. Grade 4 pushes further — two-step rules, input-output tables (function machines), and patterns hiding inside multiples and odd or even numbers. Here is the order I teach it, with a handful of counters, a notebook, and about fifteen minutes a day.

Step 1: Find the rule before you continue the pattern

The single most useful habit is to look at the gap between terms first. Ask: how do I get from one number to the next? For 5, 8, 11, 14 the gap is +3 every time. For 40, 35, 30 it is −5. Once the rule is named, continuing the sequence or filling a gap becomes almost automatic.

Not every pattern adds or subtracts, though. In 2, 4, 8, 16 the numbers double — the rule is ×2. In 81, 27, 9 the rule is divide by 3. I teach children to test add/subtract first because it is the most common, then check for multiply or divide if the numbers grow or shrink too fast for a constant gap.

Filling the gaps

A trickier task is a pattern with a hole in the middle: 6, 12, __, 24, 30. Here you find the rule from the numbers you do have (+6), then work forwards or backwards into the gap. The missing term is 18. This is exactly the skill that shows up later in algebra, so it is worth slowing down for.

Number patterns grade 4: two-step rules

This is the real Grade 4 upgrade. A two-step rule does two things to each number. Take 2, 5, 11, 23 — no constant gap works. But ‘double it, then add 1’ does: 2 becomes 5, 5 becomes 11, 11 becomes 23. Two-step rules feel like magic tricks to nine-year-olds, and that delight is useful — it makes them want to crack the next one.

My advice: describe the rule in words out loud every single time. ‘Times 3, then subtract 2.’ Saying it slows the thinking down and stops the child from guessing.

Input-output tables (function machines)

An input-output table is a rule machine. A number goes in, the rule acts on it, a new number comes out. Grade 4 children meet these as two-row or two-column tables, and they are the friendliest way I know to make the idea of a rule concrete.

Here is a function machine with the rule ‘times 3, then add 1’. Read each row: the input on the left, the output on the right.

InputRule: ×3, then +1Output
1(1 × 3) + 14
2(2 × 3) + 17
4(4 × 3) + 113
10(10 × 3) + 131

Two questions turn this from a filling exercise into real thinking. First, given an input, find the output — that is just applying the rule. Second, and harder, given an output, work backwards to the input. If the output is 22, undo the steps in reverse: subtract 1 to get 21, then divide by 3 to get 7. Working backwards is where fluency really shows.

Patterns in multiples, odd and even

Some of the best patterns are already sitting in the times tables. Look at the multiples of 5: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25 — every one ends in 5 or 0. Multiples of 2 are the even numbers; everything else is odd. These are patterns children can state as rules, and they double as quick divisibility checks.

  • Multiples of 5 end in 0 or 5.
  • Multiples of 10 end in 0.
  • Even numbers end in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8; odd numbers end in 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9.
  • Adding two even numbers always gives an even number; two odds also give an even; one of each gives an odd.
  • Square numbers 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 grow by 3, then 5, then 7 — the gaps are the odd numbers.

That last one is my favourite counter-intuitive nugget. The square numbers do not have a constant gap, yet their gaps form the neat pattern of odd numbers. Point it out and watch a curious child chase it.

Simple geometric growth

Not all growth is by adding. Fold a paper in half again and again and count the layers: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. Each step doubles — that is geometric growth, and Grade 4 is exactly when to introduce it gently alongside the add/subtract patterns. The contrast matters: a child who has only ever seen +constant patterns will assume 1, 2, 4 continues 6, 8. Showing both kinds side by side keeps them checking the rule rather than guessing.

A rule for practising rules

Pattern typeHow to spot itExample
Add / subtract a constantSame gap every step4, 9, 14, 19
Multiply / divideNumbers grow or shrink fast3, 9, 27, 81
Two-step ruleNo single gap works1, 4, 13, 40 (×3, +1)
Input-output tableA rule links each pairin 5 → out 16

One honest caveat: do not rush a child to two-step rules before single-step rules are solid. In my experience the children who struggle with function machines are almost always shaky on the times tables underneath. Fix the foundation first and the fancy patterns come easily.

Test what your child has learned

Below is a short, free quiz covering exactly these ideas — finding the rule, filling gaps, two-step rules, input-output tables, and patterns in multiples. Let your child try it, then read the explanations together for anything they miss. When they are ready for longer written practice, the printable worksheet at the end gives graded questions with a full answer key.

quiz.title: Grade 4 Number Patterns Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions on finding the rule, filling gaps, two-step rules and input-output tables. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.explanation: The rule is add 5 each time. 21 + 5 = 26.
The rule is subtract 6. 34 − 6 = 28, and 28 − 6 = 22, which fits.

questions.q: The rule is 'double it, then add 1'. Start at 3. What is next?
questions.explanation: Double 3 is 6, then add 1 to get 7.

questions.q: A function machine uses 'times 3, then add 2'. If the input is 4, what is the output?
questions.explanation: 4 times 3 is 12, then add 2 to get 14.

questions.q: Which number is a multiple of 5?
questions.explanation: Multiples of 5 end in 0 or 5. Only 45 does.
Each number is the one before times 3: 2, 6, 18, 54.

questions.q: A machine uses 'times 2, then add 3'. The output is 15. What was the input?
Look at the square numbers 1, 4, 9, 16. By how much does the pattern grow from 9 to 16?
questions.explanation: 16 − 9 = 7. The gaps between square numbers are the odd numbers 3, 5, 7.

faq.q: What are number patterns in Grade 4?
faq.a: They are sequences that follow a rule — adding or subtracting a constant, multiplying or dividing, or a two-step rule like ‘times 3, then add 1’. In Grade 4 the aim is to name the rule in words and use it, not just guess the next number.

It is a function machine on paper: a number goes in, a rule acts on it, and a new number comes out. Each row pairs an input with its output, so children practise applying a rule and working backwards from an output to the input.

faq.q: How do I teach two-step rules?
faq.a: Say the rule out loud every time, for example ‘double it, then add 1’, and do the steps in order. To find a missing input, undo the steps in reverse. Make sure the child’s times tables are solid first — that is what two-step rules lean on.

faq.q: What is the difference between Grade 3 and Grade 4 number patterns?
faq.a: Grade 3 focuses on simple growing and shape patterns with one step. Grade 4 adds two-step rules, input-output tables, and spotting patterns inside multiples, odd and even numbers, and simple doubling growth.
